extracted.intended_audience: general readers, writers, and literary scholars interested in Pulitzer Prize criteria
extracted.subtask_description: Extracts the eligibility rules, historical wording, and evaluative principles used by the Pulitzer Prize for Fiction (formerly 'Novel') — who may be considered, what forms and timeframes qualify, and the kinds of literary/moral qualities juries have cited.

rubrics_metrics.name: Eligibility — American author
rubrics_metrics.description: The prize recognizes distinguished fiction by an American author.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The award historically and currently requires the author to be American (the Plan of Award and later wording specify an 'American author'); examples in the article discuss how works with foreign settings have still qualified when the author was American (e.g., The Good Earth).

rubrics_metrics.name: Publication timeframe
rubrics_metrics.description: Works must be published during the preceding calendar year.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The prize is given annually for fiction published in the calendar year prior to the award year (the 'Year' column links to the preceding year in literature).

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguished fiction (quality standard)
rubrics_metrics.description: The prize recognizes 'distinguished fiction' — the work must be judged of outstanding literary merit.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Juries and the Advisory Board assess whether a work is 'distinguished'; when they deem no entry sufficiently distinguished the board may give no award (multiple historical examples where no award was given because no book 'imposes itself ... as demanding recognition as "distinguished fiction"').

rubrics_metrics.name: Preference — dealing with American life / 'whole(‑)some' wording
rubrics_metrics.description: The award has traditionally been given to works 'preferably dealing with American life' or 'best present[ing] the whole atmosphere of American life' (originally phrased as presenting 'the wholesome atmosphere of American life, and the highest standard of American manners and manhood').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Wording evolved over decades (original Plan of Award, 1927 change from 'wholesome' to 'whole', 1929/1936/1948 rephrasings). Despite the preference, works with non‑American settings have been awarded when deemed meritorious (e.g., Thornton Wilder's The Bridge of San Luis Rey; Pearl S. Buck's The Good Earth).

rubrics_metrics.name: Form / format — published in book form
rubrics_metrics.description: Since 1948 the prize is for 'distinguished fiction published in book form during the year by an American author.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The 1948 change explicitly limited the award to book‑form publications and widened eligibility to include short story collections and other book‑format fiction. James A. Michener's Tales of the South Pacific led to lifting a ban on short stories and expanding the category.

rubrics_metrics.name: Literary/moral evaluative considerations cited by juries
rubrics_metrics.description: Jury reports and advisory comments have invoked literary skill and moral/philosophic qualities — e.g., 'literary skill in the art of fiction', 'moral value', 'philosophic import and a spiritual elevation'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article quotes jury/advisory commentary (Richard Burton on The Bridge of San Luis Rey) showing that jurors consider not only craft but also moral/philosophic significance and 'spiritual elevation' when recommending works.

rubrics_metrics.name: Jury recommendation and Board/Advisory discretion
rubrics_metrics.description: A jury recommends winners (and in modern practice finalists), but the Advisory Board and Pulitzer Board have ultimate discretion and may accept, override, or decline to award based on their judgment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article documents multiple instances where the Advisory Board or Columbia University officials overruled jury choices, substituted other winners, or chose no award (e.g., 1941 reversal, 1974 no award despite a unanimous jury recommendation). This procedural rule affects how the evaluative criteria are applied in practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Finalists — announcement practice
rubrics_metrics.description: Finalists have been announced since 1980, usually a total of three.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Since the practice began in 1980 the process typically yields three finalists in the fiction category; this is a procedural element of how works are selected and presented to the public and boards.

rubrics_metrics.name: Possibility of shared awards or withholding the award
rubrics_metrics.description: The Board may choose to share the prize between authors or to give no award in a given year.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Historically there have been years with no award and, recently, the prize was shared for the first time in 2023. These outcomes reflect application of the 'distinguished' standard and the Board's discretion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Historical Plan of Award wording (original standard)
rubrics_metrics.description: Original Plan: 'Annually, for the American novel published during the year which shall best present the wholesome atmosphere of American life, and the highest standard of American manners and manhood.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This historic language reveals early evaluative aims (emphasis on 'wholesome'/'highest standard of American manners and manhood'); the article traces how that language was quietly changed (e.g., 1927 replacement of 'wholesome' with 'whole') and later reworded to broaden scope and reduce prescriptive moral language.
